blocks.raw: <WikiExamTable rows={[{"heading":"Urban Design Principle","description":"Definition and Application"},{"content":"Height-to-Width Ratio (H:W)","description":"Comfortable enclosure: 1:2 (building height 1, street width 2). Exposed: 1:4. Oppressive: 2:1. Measured in same units; applied to street cross-section to evaluate pedestrian comfort."},{"content":"Eyes on the Street (Jane Jacobs)","description":"Mixed uses, continuous ground-floor activity, and dense occupation create informal surveillance and pedestrian safety. Single-use, blank-walled buildings eliminate street safety. Streets are public life."},{"content":"Complete Streets","description":"Design streets for pedestrians, cyclists, transit, cars (priority order). Include sidewalks, tree canopy, seating, ground-floor activation. Prioritize accessibility; minimize car dominance."},{"content":"Townscape / Serial Vision (Gordon Cullen)","description":"Streets and spaces reveal themselves sequentially as you move through them. Enclosure, opening, visual surprises create memorable sequences. Contrast 'here' and 'there' through thoughtful building placement and street rhythm."},{"content":"Ground-Floor Activation","description":"Retail, cafés, offices, galleries at street level create vitality and safety. Residential units above enhance 24-hour presence. Contrast with blank walls (parking garages, blank building faces) that kill street life."},{"content":"Street Trees and Canopy","description":"Shade, cooling, aesthetics, air quality. Required spacing and species selection. Reduces urban heat island effect. Contributes to H:W ratio enclosure feeling."},{"content":"Pedestrian-Sclea Design","description":"Building facades show human sclea: windows, doors, texture at eye level (0–2.5m). Oversized blank panels, featureless surfaces, and windswept plazas feel hostile. Details matter."}]} />

blocks.raw: <Tip>H:W comfortable = 1:2 (not 2:1). "Eyes on the street" = Jane Jacobs (not Lynch). Complete streets = pedestrian first, car last. These three attributions are the highest-frequency urban design errors.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Inverting the H:W ratio — saying 2:1 is comfortable (oppressive), or 1:4 is oppressive (exposed) — memorize: 1:2 comfortable, 1:4 exposed, 2:1 oppressive","Attributing 'eyes on the street' to Kevin Lynch or Jan Gehl — it is Jane Jacobs' principle, from The Death and Life of Great American Cities (1961)","Confusing Kevin Lynch elements with Jane Jacobs vitality principles — Lynch describes HOW people navigate (elements); Jacobs describes WHY streets feel safe and alive (mixed use, activity)","Thinking 'complete streets' means removing cars — it means prioritizing pedestrians, cyclists, and transit over cars. Cars remain, but not dominant.","Underestimating the importance of ground-floor activation — a wide street with blank-walled buildings fails to generate 'eyes on the street' no matter how good the H:W ratio"]} />
